newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republican Congress mix of rancour, achievement.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republican Congress mix of rancour, achievement.

text.p: Two years after taking control of Congress promising "revolution," chastened Republicans prepared to leave town on Monday with a far more modest goal of saving their own political hides.

The first Republican Congress in 40 years will adjourn with a solid legislative record including historic welfare changes, telecommunications and health insurance reform, a free-market farm law, safe drinking water act, likely illegal immigration reform, line-item veto and a minimum wage increase.

But the achievements fall far short of Republicans' revolutionary rhetoric, which promised a balanced budget and sweeping structural changes to shrink the size of government and return power to individuals and the states.
The bitterly partisan session was marred by rancour, including name calling, shoving matches and general mistrust that prevented productive work for most of last year.

Political analysts called the 104th Congress a political failure for Republicans, who overreached by pushing for more sweeping changes in popular middle-class entitlements like Medicare and student aid than voters would accept.

Democrats scored political points by savaging the Republicans on Medicare and attacking controversial House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich. Gingrich dominated Congress in the early days, but moved into the background this year beleagured by ethics problems and his own political missteps.

"On purely political terms the Republican majority failed. The broad political objective was to reassure the American people that the Republicans were worthy of their trust," said Thomas Mann, an expert at the Brookings Institution. "On grounds of legislative productivity, this is a very successful Congress."

In a telling sign that the Republican revolution had faded, the House's final act was to approve $6.5 billion in extra domestic spending President Bill Clinton demanded as part of a massive bill to keep the federal government operating.

That stood in stark contrast to possibly the most enduring image of this Congress -- two government shutdowns last winter engineered by Republicans in an unsuccessful, and unpopular, effort to force Clinton into a balanced budget deal.

Eager to avoid a repeat and anxious to return home to campaign, Republicans gave in to the White House. In a sign of their haste to leave Washington, the expected Sept. 30 adjournment would be the earliest since 1976.

Still, House Republicans claimed the session was one of the most successful in recent years, saying they kept their promise to cut government and pass their 10-part Contract with America in 100 days, though much of it never became law.
